nodes.body:
Interlinking lets us take a reference to a function in a docstring (or qmd), and render it as a link to the function's documentation. This could be a link either within the current documentation (e.g. quartodoc docs) or across documentation sites (e.g. to python.org/docs).

**Key pieces:**

* generate a sphinx inventory file (or something similar)
* figure out a quarto strategy for interlinking (e.g. a filter?)

**Examples:**

* [plotnine geom_bar api doc](https://plotnine.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generated/plotnine.geoms.geom_bar.html#plotnine.geoms.geom_bar)
* [py-shiny page_fixed api doc](https://shiny.rstudio.com/py/api/reference/shiny.ui.page_fixed.html)

Note the "See Also" section, and links from annotations in these pages..

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2574498/200365980-b3f13f1b-fae0-49b6-b464-8534cb0cbb32.png)


## Sphinx inventory files

A sphinx inventory file maps function names (or class member, etc..) to their internal pages on a documentation site. It is a sort-of gzipped file, and its structure is essentially:

* `"<object_type>": { <name>: <internal_url> }`

See this the [sphinx inventory case study](https://github.com/machow/quartodoc/blob/main/case_studies/sphinx-inventory.md) for how to read and use these files.

## Quarto interlinking

From what I've gathered, there are two ways we could do interlinking:

* when generating a qmd: quartodoc generates a reference page w/ links already generated. This would restrict us to interlinking only references in docstrings.
* during qmd rendering: quarto maybe could do interlinking through [filters](https://quarto.org/docs/extensions/filters.html)?

## Extra: how does pkgdown interlink?

[pkgdown](https://pkgdown.r-lib.org/) is an R package that can handle interlinking (note it does not use quarto).

It interlinks by the following strategy:

* generate a `_pkgdown.yml` file with with a reference section, that lists out all doc API functions.
* for crosslinking to other doc sites...
  - use `_pkgdown.yml` or the DESCRIPTION file to get the URL to the doc site
  - afaict assumes function docs have url of form: `{SITE_URL}/reference/{function_name}`. (e.g. see [this downlit code](https://github.com/r-lib/downlit/blob/d5622d665ebe4d3529b297aa926fe3c0132c8b81/R/metadata.R#L6))

griffe uses statics analysis to get objects and their docstrings, so some kinds of dynamically generated docstrings won't be found. 

For example:

* siuba uses the `functools.partial` function to define `inner_join` as `partial(join, ...)`.
* plotnine uses a decorator ([`@document`](https://github.com/has2k1/plotnine/blob/main/plotnine/doctools.py#L552)) to fill in common pieces from a template (e.g. [geom_bar](https://github.com/has2k1/plotnine/blob/main/plotnine/geoms/geom_bar.py#L6))
* py-shiny uses a decorator ([`@add_example()`](https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/blob/165d698871a4e63f83d0943b881ffb78e89f6f74/shiny/_docstring.py#L25)) for similar reasons (e.g. [isolate](https://github.com/rstudio/py-shiny/blob/main/shiny/reactive/_core.py#L193-L195))

Let's allow a hook for handling these situations at render time:

* `MdRenderer(..., pre_docstring:  Callable[griffe.dataclasses.Object, griffe.dataclasses.Object])`
* user can e.g. get the name off the object, do dynamic work (like import the object directly) and do anything needed like setting the `.docstring` attribute.
* (Alternatively, we could let someone return a string that is the docstring to be parsed?)

siuba provides a tree formatter that displays a compact representation of the data / hierarchy.
It seems like a visitor that renders a parsed docstring to the format (while truncating strings) would be useful for seeing the structure of the docstring (e.g. classes, nesting, tiny peek at content).

```python
from siuba import _

(_.x + _.y).mean()
```

**output**

```
█─'__call__'
└─█─.
  ├─█─+
  │ ├─█─.
  │ │ ├─_
  │ │ └─'x'
  │ └─█─.
  │   ├─_
  │   └─'y'
  └─'mean'
```

### edit: here's a template to get started

```python
import griffe.dataclasses as dc
import griffe.docstrings.dataclasses as ds

from plum import dispatch
from typing import Union


class TreePreviewer:

    def __init__(self, n_spaces = 2):
        self.n_spaces = n_spaces

    @dispatch
    def visit(self, el):
        raise NotImplementedError(f"Unsupported type: {type(el)}")

    @dispatch
    def visit(self, el: Union[dc.Alias, dc.Object]):
        res = [
            "NAME:" + el.name,                     # just a string
            "PARAMETERS: " + self.visit(el.parameters),
            "SECTIONS: " + self.visit(el.docstring)
        ]
        
        # return something pretty
        return "\n".join(res)
    
    @dispatch
    def visit(self, el: dc.Parameters):
        return "parameters..."
    
    @dispatch
    def visit(self, el: dc.Docstring):
        res = [self.visit(child) for child in el.parsed]
        
        # make pretty
        
        # return something useful
        return ", ".join(res)
    
    @dispatch
    def visit(self, el: dc.DocstringSection):
        return "docstring section"
```

**Example:**

```python
from quartodoc import get_object
previewer = TreePreviewer(2)

print(previewer.visit(get_object("quartodoc", "get_object")))
```

```
NAME:get_object
PARAMETERS: parameters...
SECTIONS: docstring section, docstring section, docstring section, docstring section
```

Many python documentation sites also include their API doc pages on a sidebar, but this currently requires users do a lot of manual work. They can use quarto's options for [auto sidebar generation](https://quarto.org/docs/websites/website-navigation.html#auto-generation), but this only supports these two cases:

* contents are all laid flat on the sidebar
* contents are laid out in sections, by assuming each folder is a sidebar section

However, this means that sidebar layout and file directory structure are coupled. In practice, python documentation sites often lay out function pages flat in an API folder (e.g. [pandas.tseries.offsets.DateOffset.html](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.tseries.offsets.DateOffset.html)).

## Thoughts on fixes

* If quarto could decouple them (e.g. by allowing a sidebar config file, like `references/_sidebar.yml` etc..), then quartodoc could generate the sidebar config for references.
* quartodoc could add an option to output files in nested directories.
* quartodoc could print out the piece that users would paste into their `_quarto.yml`.

It seems like only the first will allow people to port their doc sites, without changing their structures. (Note also that the structure of python API sidebars generally does not correspond to package structure)

## Example 

For example, here is @isabelizimm's work on porting the vetiver docs to quartodoc. Notice that each section of the reference index page is also included on the sidebar.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2574498/213519396-d688ad64-7744-4744-be4f-81f1a16c39c8.png)

Currently, this must be done manually, by hard-coding the sidebar in `_quart.yml`:

```yaml
project:
  type: website

format:
  html:
    toc: true


website:
  title: "Vetiver API docs"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: reference/index.qmd
        text: Reference

  # note the duplication between sidebar and quartodoc fields
  #
  sidebar:
    - id: reference
      title: Reference
      contents:
        - section: Version
          contents:
            - reference/VetiverModel.qmd
            - reference/vetiver_pin_write.qmd
        # ...

quartodoc:
  style: pkgdown
  dir: reference
  package: vetiver
  sections:
    - title: "Version"
      desc: ""
      contents:
        - VetiverModel
        - vetiver_pin_write
      # ...
```

Currently, people using quartodoc must perform three steps (see [getting started](https://machow.github.io/quartodoc/get-started/overview.html), and [interlinks docs](https://machow.github.io/quartodoc/get-started/interlinks.html#running-the-interlinks-filter)):

```
# create documentation pages
python -m quartodoc build

# create sphinx inventory files
python -m quartodoc interlinks

quarto preview
```

Ideally the quartodoc steps should be run at this frequency (they may take seconds to perform):

* build: every time the source documentation changes, or once (e.g. when you first run quarto preview)
* interlinks: once

This means that the pre-render field isn't a great choice, as it runs before any page renders. With project types there is the serve option, which may get us what we need?

One thing that is confusing is that `quartodoc` has a section in the `_quarto.yml` file, but `quartodoc` is not actually a quarto extension.

There is a two-step build process to build the documentation for a python module with quartodoc:
- Run `quartodoc build` to generate .qmd files from the .py source files.
- Run `quarto render` to convert the .qmd files to .html

It took me a while to fully understand the consequences of this -- for example, changing the `quartodoc` section of `_quarto.yml` does _not_ trigger a rebuild when `quarto preview` is running.

I've thought about it a bit, and I think it would be clearer if the `quartodoc` configuration was in a separate file from `_quarto.yml`, to make it clear to users that running `quarto` has nothing to do with running `quartodoc`.

When the returns section of a docstring is a single entry. @wch mentioned that it might be useful to format it as something than other than a table.

For example, the docstring:

```
from quartodoc import MdRenderer
from griffe.docstrings.parsers import parse_numpy
from griffe.dataclasses import Docstring

renderer = MdRenderer()

doc = Docstring("""
Returns
--------
result : str
    Some string that represents something cool.
""")

parsed = parse_numpy(doc)

print(renderer.render(parsed[0]))
```

```markdown
| Type   | Description                                 |
|--------|---------------------------------------------|
| str    | Some string that represents something cool. |
```

@wch do you mind specifying how type and description should be rendered, if there is only a single entry? Something like this?

```
Returns
--------

**<type>**: <description>
```

Note that other output approaches, like the one used by the pydata theme might also address this, by being less table-ly looking (e.g. see results on [this pandas api page](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.keys.html))

Currently, users need to...

* run `python -m quartodoc build --verbose`
* run `quarto preview`
* after tweaking docs, re-run the first command

I've noticed that this has two negative effects:

* **starting is a bit slow**: all the useful stuff happens after the second command
* **update paralysis**: after people tweak the quartodoc section of `_quarto.yml`, or modify a docstring in their source code, it takes a bit to remember how to get the preview to update.

A watch command could resolve this by:

* having an optional flag to also start `quarto preview`, so a user only needs to run one thing.
* watching the source directory, and rebuilding docstrings when it changes.

Carlos mentioned it could be named quartodog. I think we should definitely have a `quartodoc watch` command, but also shouldn't rule out the value of a dog themed quartodog version.

Currently, users are able to document class attributes using the numpy `Attributes` docstring section.

E.g.

```python
class SomeClass:
    """a class

    Attributes
    ----------
    a:
        The a attribute
    b:
        The b attribute
    """

    a: int

    def __init__(self, b: int):
        self.b = b
```

However, we don't have great automatic handling for class attributes defined like...

```python
class SomeClass:
    """a class"""

    a: int
    """The a attribute"""

    def __init__(self, b: int):
        self.b = b
        """The b attribute"""

    @property
    def c(self):
        """The c attribute, which is really a descriptor"""
```

I don't think this is a huge for people designing their API docs from scratch, since they can use the Attributes section to get what they want. However, it is an issue for people porting their documentation over from sphinx, or who expect to document in this way.

## Design considerations

* **Full docstrings**. While the Attributes docstring section can be rendered as a table, the individual attribute docstrings approach can create full docstrings--e.g. with a Notes, Returns section, etc...---which makes them more like method documentation.
* **Confusing there are 2 attribute doc approaches**. We will need to handle expectations around things like what should happen if both docstring approaches are used at the same time.
* **Presentation**. We'll need to figure out how to present and group attributes. mkdocstrings seems to do a really great job here.

Currently, several pages of our documentation rely on creating griffe objects to represent python objects. For example, the [Common Issues and Examples page](https://machow.github.io/quartodoc/get-started/docstring-examples.html) presents functions with docstrings. In addition, many pages use `get_object("quartodoc", "get_object")` as a way of fetching an example object.

However, there are two big challenges with this:

* Just getting the data for some object you define is not easy. Generally, I save my code into a .py file--like `test_file.py`--then load it using `get_object("test_file")`.
* Navigating trees of data about python objects feels complex

I wonder if there are two ways we could make this easier:

* **quick loading**: make it quick to load objects from a string without the user writing to a file
* **cheatsheat**: overlay all the data type names on top of an example function with a docstring?


## How griffe handles quick loading

griffe has some neat functionality for handling this in tests, using a function called `temporary_inspected_module()`.

<details>
    <summary>code for `temporary_inspected_module()`</summary>

```python
# this code is copied from https://github.com/mkdocstrings/griffe/blob/master/tests/helpers.py

import tempfile
import sys

from griffe.agents.visitor import visit
from griffe.agents.inspector import inspect
from importlib import invalidate_caches
from pathlib import Path
from textwrap import dedent
from contextlib import contextmanager
from typing import Iterator, Mapping, Sequence
from griffe.dataclasses import Module, Object


@contextmanager
def temporary_pyfile(code: str) -> Iterator[tuple[str, Path]]:
    """Create a module.py file containing the given code in a temporary directory.

    Parameters:
        code: The code to write to the temporary file.

    Yields:
        module_name: The module name, as to dynamically import it.
        module_path: The module path.
    """
    # TODO: Michael removed TMPDIR_PREFIX
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as tmpdir:
        tmpfile = Path(tmpdir) / "module.py"
        tmpfile.write_text(dedent(code))
        yield "module", tmpfile


@contextmanager
def temporary_inspected_module(code: str) -> Iterator[Module]:
    """Create and inspect a temporary module with the given code.

    Parameters:
        code: The code of the module.

    Yields:
        The inspected module.
    """
    with temporary_pyfile(code) as (name, path):
        try:
            yield inspect(name, filepath=path)

        # TODO: Michael added this except clause
        except Exception as e:
            print(e)

        finally:
            del sys.modules["module"]
            invalidate_caches()


```

</details>

```python
code = '''
def my_func(a: int):
    """Some docstring"""
    return 1
'''

with temporary_inspected_module(code) as mod:
    my_func = mod.members["my_func"]

print(my_func)
```

## Background

Compound types don't always interlink consistently because of the nuances of Python's typing system.  The failure modes on compound data type interlinking are confusing and distracting for the end user.  See examples below.

### Example 1 `spellcheck`

From [these shiny docs](https://shiny.rstudio.com/py/api/ui.input_text.html#parameters), see the last row in the below table, the compound type doesn't render consistently.

![image](https://github.com/machow/quartodoc/assets/1483922/d0549670-07db-46a2-9378-efec6e8ba6fd)

### Example 2: `object_name`

See the second row in the below table which will render as `str | None` because of the way this compound type is annotated in Griffe.

![image](https://github.com/machow/quartodoc/assets/1483922/4c59d3b1-8660-4ea2-a6af-e5cc27f0e82c)

#### Can we fix this?

We would have to make lots of upstream changes to Griffe, and it's not clear if this is desired in this situation.  More importantly its not clear that the effort is worth it, which is why we outlined the below three options

## Decision
There are three options:

1. Turn **interlinking off by default** completely (not even names)
2. Have two options: `names | all` 
   - `names`: would just render names like `MyType` and not compound types like `[List[Union[str, int], CustomType]` because this is brittle and has failure modes that can be confusing for end users when things don't interlink properly.  If you want a compound type to be rendered you would set the type equal to a variable like `MyType = [List[Union[str, int], CustomType]`
   - `all`: this is where we attempt to aggressively interlink everything, including compound types.
3. Only interlink named types and not compound types (Hamel's favorite).  This is the same as `#2` but doesn't allow for an option and just make this how quartodoc "works".  See "Hamel's Opinion" below for more explanation.

#### Hamel's Opinion:

I think we should render names only and not have any options.  If there are are compound types we should set them equal to a variable `MyType = [List[Union[str, int], CustomType]` and then that will render.  I think having too many options (`#2` above) is confusing!   I believe that if a compound type is "important" enough, that should either be a DataClass or assigned to a variable.

From @juliasilge, our sanitize function escapes characters that could break rendered pieces like tables. It also escapes `[` and `]` so that type annotations will not be interpreted as footnotes. However, because the same sanitization is applied to the parameters table, it breaks interlinks.

For example:

```python
from quartodoc.renderers.base import sanitize

sanitize("I am a link to [get_object](`quartodoc.get_object`)")

# result: I am a link to \[get_object\](`quartodoc.get_object`)
```

Let's separate out sanitization into two functions:

* `sanitize_table_entry()`: escape `\n` and `|`
* `sanitize_annotation()`: escape `\n`, `|` ,`[`, `]`

Down the road we can potentially clean this all up by generating things another way.

Large inventory files slow the interlinks filter. For sites with many pages (e.g. 100+), this can substantially increase build times.

## Background

quartodoc uses this process for handling interlinks:

* Running [`quartodoc interlinks`](https://machow.github.io/quartodoc/get-started/interlinks.html) downloads inventory files, and saves them as as json (e.g. `_inv/python_objects.json`)
* The interlinks lua filter ([installation](https://machow.github.io/quartodoc/get-started/interlinks.html#installing), [code](https://github.com/machow/quartodoc/blob/main/_extensions/interlinks/interlinks.lua)) does this for each page being rendered:
  - reads the json files
  - replaces any uses of interlinks syntax with links derived from the json files

However, this raises the following challenges:

* **io, parsing**: the files must be read and parsed every time a file is rendered. This delay can add up over a lot of files.
* **lookup**: currently, we loop over every entry when looking up a link. This is inefficient, but I suspect fast in human time.

inventories like [statsmodels.org](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/objects.inv) are 10MB unzipped, and have ~40,000 entries, so they're not a huge time sink, but it adds up when multiplied by number of files. From what I can tell, **it takes the lua filter ~.75 seconds just to read and parse this file (mostly due to parsing json)**.

## Example

Run the following on the files below:

* `quartodoc interlinks` (creates `_inv` folder with inventory files as json)
* `quarto render example.qmd --to gfm --output --`

**`_quarto.yml`**:

```yaml
filters:
  - interlinks

# interlinks are slow
interlinks:
  sources:
    python:
      url: https://docs.python.org/3/
    statsmodels:
      url: https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/
#   matplotlib:
#     url: https://matplotlib.org/stable/
#   mizani:
#     url: https://mizani.readthedocs.io/stable/
#   numpy:
#     url: https://numpy.org/doc/stable/
#   scipy:
#     url: https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/
#   pandas:
#     url: https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/
#   sklearn:
#     url: https://scikit-learn.org/stable/
#   skmisc:
#     url: https://has2k1.github.io/scikit-misc/stable/
#   adjustText:
#     url: https://adjusttext.readthedocs.io/en/latest/
#   patsy:
#      url: https://patsy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/
```

**example.qmd**:

``````
---
---

[](`statsmodels.base.distributed_estimation`)

``````


## Potential Solutions

In order of complexity:

* speed up parsing
  - find a way to parse the json files faster, OR
  - use a format that takes advantage of the fact that this data has a fixed structure (e.g. similar to a SQL table)
* provide some kind of persistence (and only parse once)
  - e.g. run a webserver during site rendering, serve data or answers over a file socket.
  - e.g. as an extreme example we have a "we need something redis-like" problem, due to quarto's rendering approach.
  - (other tools like sphinx or mkdocs provide these mechanisms out of the box)
nodes.title: Interlinks filter: support extremely large inventory files

Noticed in pyshiny, when a function is an alias to an alias, then the signature gets rendered incorrectly.

This happens when you...

1. import something from a submodule (`shiny.ui.dataframe._dataframe.output_data_frame`), and then
2. import again from that submodule (`shiny.ui.dataframe.output_data_frame`)
3. use a final import in the reference (`shiny.ui.output_data_frame`)
 
In this case, quartodoc should render the signature using name (3), but is using name (2).

https://shiny.posit.co/py/api/ui.output_data_frame.html

```python
from quartodoc import Auto, blueprint

auto = blueprint(Auto(name = "ui.output_data_frame", package="shiny"))

# an alias
auto.obj

# also an alias
auto.obj.target

# finally the target
auto.obj.target.target
```

The fix is pretty quick, we just need to fully resolve the alias in `Renderer.signature`.

## Problem

When I only import attributes (and specify them to `__all__`) in a rendered, quartodoc ignores them and doesn't render its documentation.

```python
# module.py

from othermodule import CONSTANT, NOT_SHOWN_CONSTANT

__all__ = ["CONSTANT"]
```

```yaml
# _quarto.yaml
quartodoc:
  ...
  sections:
    - title: Some title
      contents:
        - module
```

This is a problem because often in packages you have "private part of the package", and you only expose the "public" part via imports like that. For example you have a structure like this:

```
package/
  subpackage/
    __init__.py  # everything imported in here
    _internal.py 
```

## Solution

Similar to `pdoc`: what to render can be decided based on contents of `__all__`. For example `NOT_SHOWN_CONSTANT` shouldn't be rendered because it is not in `__all__`.

Generally, dynamic loading works well for modules, classes and functions, but can behave surprisingly for instances. This is because what it means to document an instance is ambiguous.

Consider below:

```python
# Functions ----

def some_func():
    """I am a docstring"""

some_dynamic_func = some_func

some_other_dynamic_func = some_func
"""I am a function"""



# Instances ----

some_int = 1

some_other_int = 2
"""Another int"""
```

Note that dynamically loading produces these behaviors:

* **functions**: when documenting any of the functions above (some_func, some_dynamic_fun, some_other_dynamic_func) the docstring `some_func.__doc__` is used.
* **instances**: when documenting `some_int` or `some_other_int`, the underlying docstring `int.__doc__` is also used. 
  - However, this can feel surprising and wrong, because the user took the time to use the special docstring format on `some_other_int`.

For cases where a variable has a docstring defined below it, we should favor that docstring, so it matches what happens statically.

The current way interlinks are specified is adapted directly from the [Intersphinx](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/usage/extensions/intersphinx.html) extension. This format uses [reStructuredText Interpreted Text Role](https://docutils.sourceforge.io/docs/ref/rst/roles.html) where, the colons and the backticks matter because the combination triggers the processing.

quartodoc implements interlinks using pandoc filters and the processing is triggered on markdown links where what matters is:

1. The link-target matches our spec
2. We can process the tokens in the target from right to left

So we do not need the combination of colons and backticks. We can do with only colons. Here is a comparison

|     | Intersphinx                                     | Current Interlink                                   | Proposed Interlink                             |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------- |
|  1  |                                                 | `` [](`target`) ``                                  | `[](:target:)`                                 |
|  2  | `` :reftype:`target` ``                         | `` [](:reftype:`target`) ``                         | `[](:reftype:target:)`                         |
|  3  | `` :domain:reftype:`target` ``                  | `` [](:domain:reftype:`target`) ``                  | `[](:domain:reftype:target:)`                  |
|  4  | `` :external:domain:reftype:`target` ``         | `` [](:external:domain:reftype:`target`) ``         | `[](:external:domain:reftype:target:)`         |
|  5  | `` :external+invname:domain:reftype:`target` `` | `` [](:external+invname:domain:reftype:`target`) `` | `[](:external+invname:domain:reftype:target:)` |
|  6  | `` :domain:reftype:`text<target>` ``            | `` [text](:domain:reftype:`target`) ``              | `[text](:domain:reftype:target:)`              |

Given the differences in processing Intersphinx format cannot (usually) represent only a target (case 1). And the translation rule to copy the Intersphinx stuff into the braces of a markdown link does not apply to all cases. We have a more natural solution for case 6.

While at best this saves us a single character, backticks are also a markdown syntax element and the proposed change invites less visual scrutiny and looks better without them.

This change can be implemented without affecting the current users. The current style may be dropped silently at first then deprecated with a warning.

**Some Context**

Griffe provides the ability to distinguish between Objects and Aliases, where an Alias arises out of any reference to an object by a path that is not it's canonical_path. i.e. any imported Objects become Aliases.

Understandably, there after the difference between Objects and Aliases has to do with the names and paths.

**Issue**

In quartodoc, Objects and Aliases have another difference. By default, referring to an Object includes all members of the Object, while for an Alias the members of the target Object are excluded.

This means that in the config, using an Alias path is burdensome since we have to explicitly list the members. As an Alias path may be the recommended API path to an object, Aliases when listed in the config should be treated the same as Objects.

On the whole Aliases should only be treated differently if they are implicit.

For example.

1. In a config file, using an Alias is an explicit action
2. In a module, listing an Alias in `module.__all__` is an explicit action, since `__all__` defines the public members of the module.

**Demonstration of the problem**
```python
from quartodoc import blueprint, Auto,

doc1 = blueprint(Auto(name="pandas:DataFrame"))  # API Path (Alias)
doc2 = blueprint(Auto(name="pandas.core.frame:DataFrame"))  # Canonical Path (Object)

len(doc1.members), len(doc2.members)
```

```
0, 137
```

That means to document `pandas.DataFrame` and all of its members at the recommended API point, you would have to list 137 members.
nodes.title: On the difference between Objects and Aliases

Hi! Thanks for the awesome package.

The [Numpydoc specification for Parameters](https://numpydoc.readthedocs.io/en/latest/format.html#parameters) uses a space on both sides of the colon between the variable name and type, as in 
```
Parameters
----------
x : int
```
When I follow Numpydoc and include a space on each side of the colon in docstrings, I get extra parentheses in the quartodoc output:
![image](https://github.com/machow/quartodoc/assets/25447423/0f2866e5-8d81-46ac-b40e-59969d630c3f)


The Numpydocs make it seem that a docstring like
```
Parameters
----------
x: int
```
is wrong (eventhough I prefer it). But in this case, the extraneous parentheses do not appear in the quartodoc output:
![image](https://github.com/machow/quartodoc/assets/25447423/409e49f7-18e9-42e6-9bfc-1b7cabdd5c4d)

Is this a feature or a bug?
